title.en: The Creative Principle Which Is Itself Uncreated (Liezi)
title.zh: 有生不生，有化不化（列子天瑞篇）

region.en: Lieh Tzŭ's plot of ground in Chêng (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: Lieh Tzŭ repeats Hu Ch'iu Tzŭ-lin's teaching: there is a Creative Principle which is itself uncreated, a Principle of Change which is itself unchanging; the Uncreated is able to create life, the Unchanging to effect change — self-engendered and self-evolved, it would be a mistake to call it by any one of its names.
summary.zh: 有生不生，有化不化；不生者能生生，不化者能化化——自生自化，自形自色。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Taishang zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: There is a Creative Principle which is itself uncreated; there is a Principle of Change which is itself unchanging. The Uncreated is able to create life; the Unchanging is able to effect change. That which is produced cannot but continue producing; that which is evolved cannot but continue evolving. Hence there is constant production and constant evolution. The law of constant production and of constant evolution at no time ceases to operate. So is it with the Yin and the Yang, so is it with the Four Seasons.

That, then, which engenders all things is itself unengendered; that by which all things are evolved is itself untouched by evolution. Self-engendered and self-evolved, it has in itself the elements of substance, appearance, wisdom, strength, dispersion and cessation. Yet it would be a mistake to call it by any one of these names.

title.en: Heaven and Earth Engendered Out of Nothing (Liezi)
title.zh: 天地安從生：渾淪與清濁（列子天瑞篇）

region.en: The Great Change before substance (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 太易之初（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: The Liezi's great cosmogonic sequence: the Great Change, the Great Origin, the Great Beginning, the Great Primordial Simplicity — until substance, form, and essential qualities still blended together is called Chaos. Then the purer and lighter elements, tending upwards, made the Heavens; the grosser and heavier, tending downwards, made the Earth; and substance, harmoniously proportioned, became Man.
summary.zh: 太易、太初、太始、太素——形質混而不離，謂之渾淪；清輕者上為天，重濁者下為地，沖和氣者為人。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; a priority Creation & Cosmology narrative — the tai-chi sequence that later Cosmological Daoism systematised. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The inspired men of old regarded the Yin and the Yang as the cause of the sum total of Heaven and Earth. But that which has substance is engendered from that which is devoid of substance; out of what then were Heaven and Earth engendered? They were engendered out of nothing, and came into existence of themselves.

Hence we say, there is a great Principle of Change, a great Origin, a great Beginning, a great Primordial Simplicity. In the great Change substance is not yet manifest. In the great Origin lies the beginning of substance. In the great Beginning, lies the beginning of material form. In the great Simplicity lies the beginning of essential qualities.

When substance, form and essential qualities are still indistinguishably blended together it is called Chaos. Chaos means that all things are chaotically intermixed and not yet separated from one another. The purer and lighter elements, tending upwards, made the Heavens; the grosser and heavier elements, tending downwards, made the Earth. Substance, harmoniously proportioned, became Man; and, Heaven and Earth containing thus a spiritual element, all things were evolved and produced.

title.en: Why the Dead Are Called 'Men Who Have Returned' (Liezi)

region.en: Lieh Tzŭ's plot of ground in Chêng (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: The spiritual element in man is allotted by Heaven, the corporeal frame by Earth; when the spirit parts from the body each returns to its proper place — that is why disembodied spirits are called kuei, which means 'returning,' returning to their true dwelling-place. And the Yellow Emperor said: If my spirit returns through the gates whence it came, where does the Ego continue to exist?
summary.zh: 精神者天之分，骨骸者地之分——精神離形，各歸其真，故謂之鬼；鬼，歸也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the kuei=returning etymology is the aition of the Chinese word for ghost. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The spiritual element in man is allotted to him by Heaven, his corporeal frame by Earth. The part that belongs to Heaven is ethereal and dispersive, the part that belongs to Earth is dense and tending to conglomeration. When the spirit parts from the body, each of these elements returns to its proper place. That is why disembodied spirits are called kuei, which means "returning," that is, returning to their true dwelling-place.

The Yellow Emperor said: "If my spirit returns through the gates whence it came, and my bones go back to the source from which they sprang, where does the Ego continue to exist?" Between his birth and his latter end, man passes through four chief stages of development:--infancy, adolescence, old age and death. In infancy, the vital force is concentrated, the will is simple, and the general harmony of the system is perfect. ... In death, he comes to his rest, and returns to the Absolute.

title.en: The Old Man in Deerskin Who Was Happy Three Ways (Liezi)
title.zh: 泰山之叟，被裘擊壤（列子天瑞篇）

region.en: The wilds of Mount T'ai (Shandong, China)

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: Over Mount T'ai Confucius finds an aged man in a deerskin girded with rope, singing as he plays on a lute — happy for three grounds: it has fallen to his lot to be a man, the noblest of God's creations; to be a male; and to have walked the earth for ninety years. Poverty is the normal lot of the scholar, death the appointed end for all human beings.
summary.zh: 孔子遊於泰山，見裘公聲然操琴——天生萬物，唯人為貴；既得為人，是一樂也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Confucius was travelling once over Mount T'ai when he caught sight of an aged man roaming in the wilds. He was clothed in a deerskin, girded with a rope, and was singing as he played on a lute. "My friend," said Confucius, "what is it that makes you so happy?" The old man replied: "I have a great deal to make me happy. God created all things, and of all His creations man is the noblest. It has fallen to my lot to be a man: that is my first ground for happiness. Then, there is a distinction between male and female, the former being rated more highly than the latter. Therefore it is better to be a male; and since I am one, I have a second ground for happiness.

Furthermore, some are born who never behold the sun or the moon, and who never emerge from their swaddling-clothes. But I have already walked the earth for the space of ninety years. That is my third ground for happiness. Poverty is the normal lot of the scholar, death the appointed end for all human beings. Abiding in the normal state, and reaching at last the appointed end, what is there that should make me unhappy?" "What an excellent thing it is," cried Confucius, "to be able to find a source of consolation in oneself!"

title.en: Great Indeed Is Death: Tzŭ Kung Yearns for Rest (Liezi)
title.zh: 大哉死乎：子貢厭學（列子天瑞篇）

region.en: The graves in the wilds (symbolic pin: Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 原野之墳（象徵定位：山東曲阜）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: Tzŭ Kung, tired of philosophy, yearns for rest; Confucius points to all the graves, vaults, tombs, and funeral urns. Great indeed is Death! exclaims Tzŭ Kung — it gives rest to the noble-hearted and causes the base to cower. Men feel the joy of life, but do not realise its bitterness; they think of the evils of death, but not of the repose which it confers. And the dead are men who have returned.
summary.zh: 子貢倦於學，告仲尼曰：願有所息——大哉死乎！君子息焉，小人休焉。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Tzu Kung was tired of philosophy, and confided his feelings to Confucius, saying: "I yearn for rest." Confucius replied: "In life there is no rest." "Is rest, then, nowhere to be found?" "Oh, yes!" replied Confucius; "look at all the graves in the wilds, all the vaults, all the tombs, all the funeral urns, and you may know where rest is to be found." "Great, indeed, is Death!" exclaimed Tzu Kung. "It gives rest to the noble-hearted, and causes the base to cower." "You are right," said Confucius. "Men feel the joy of life, but do not realise its bitterness. They feel the weariness of old age, but not its peacefulness. They think of the evils of death, but not of the repose which it confers."

The ancients spoke of the dead as kuei-jen (men who have returned). But if the dead are men who have returned, the living are men on a journey. Those who are on a journey and think not of returning have cut themselves off from their home. Should any one man cut himself off from his home, he would incur universal reprobation. But all mankind being homeless, there is none to see the error.

title.en: The Man Who Feared the Sky Would Fall (Liezi)

region.en: The State of Ch'i (Linzi, Shandong, China)

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: A man of Ch'i is so afraid the universe will collapse and fall to pieces that he can neither sleep nor eat. Heaven is only an accumulation of ether, says his enlightener; the sun, moon and stars are bright lights within that mass; the earth is an agglomeration of matter filling the four corners of space — why be afraid? And Ch'ang Lu Tzŭ laughs at both: Heaven and earth must of necessity pass away, but neither will revert to destruction apart from the other.
summary.zh: 杞國有人憂天地崩墜，身亡所寄，廢寢食者——天，積氣耳；亡處亡氣。地，積塊耳；充塞四虛。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the 'worry of Ch'i' (Ch'i-jen yu-t'ien) became a proverb for needless alarm. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: There was once a man in the Ch'i State who was so afraid the universe would collapse and fall to pieces, leaving his body without a lodgment, that he could neither sleep nor eat. Another man, pitying his distress, went to enlighten him. "Heaven," he said, "is nothing more than an accumulation of ether, and there is no place where ether is not. Processes of contraction and expansion, inspiration and expiration are continually taking place up in the heavens. Why then should you be afraid of a collapse?" "It is true that Heaven is an accumulation of ether; but the sun, the moon, and the stars -- will they not fall down upon us?" "Sun, moon and stars are likewise only bright lights within this mass of ether. Even supposing they were to fall, they could not possibly harm us by their impact."

"But what if the earth should fall to pieces?" "The earth," replied the other, "is merely an agglomeration of matter, which fills and blocks up the four corners of space. There is no part of it where matter is not. All day long there is constant treading and tramping on the surface of the earth. Why then should you be afraid of its falling to pieces?" Thereupon the man was relieved of his fears and rejoiced exceedingly. But Ch'ang Lu Tzu laughed at them both, saying: "Knowing these facts, who can say that they will never be destroyed? Heaven and earth must of necessity pass away, but neither will revert to destruction apart from the other. Who, having to face the day of disruption, would not be alarmed?"

The Master Lieh Tzu heard of the discussion, and smiling said: "He who maintains that Heaven and earth are destructible, and he who upholds the contrary, are both equally at fault. Whether they are destructible or not is something we can never know. The living and the dead, the going and the coming, know nothing of each other's state. Whether destruction awaits the world or no, why should I trouble my head about it?"

title.en: Mr. Kuo the Good Thief of Heaven and Earth (Liezi)
title.zh: 齊國國氏善為盜（列子天瑞篇）

region.en: The road from Sung to Ch'i (Shangqiu to Linzi, China)
region.zh: 宋適齊之道（商丘至臨淄）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: Mr. Hsiang the poor man asks Mr. Kuo the rich for the secret of his prosperity: it is because I am a good thief — stealing the riches of Heaven and earth each in their season, the fertilising rain-water from the clouds, the natural products of mountain and meadow. The literal thief climbs walls and is stripped of all he has; Tung Kuo the learned explains that we are all thieves of the harmony of the Yin and Yang in order to keep alive.
summary.zh: 國氏曰：吾善為盜——盜天之時，盜陰陽之和，若耳目鼻口；向氏踰垣鑿室而盜，被殘而歸。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The latter travelled from Sung to Ch'i and asked the other for the secret of his prosperity. Mr. Kuo told him. "It is because I am a good thief," he said. "The first year I began to be a thief, I had just enough. The second year, I had ample. The third year, I reaped a great harvest. And, in course of time, I found myself the owner of whole villages and districts." Mr. Hsiang was overjoyed; he understood the word "thief" in its literal sense, but he did not understand the true way of becoming a thief. Accordingly, he climbed over walls and broke into houses, grabbing everything he could see or lay hands upon. But before very long his thefts brought him into trouble, and he was stripped even of what he had previously possessed.

Now let me put you on the right track. We all know that Heaven has its seasons, and that earth has its riches. Well, the things that I steal are the riches of Heaven and earth, each in their season -- the fertilising rain-water from the clouds, and the natural products of mountain and meadow-land. Thus I grow my grain and ripen my crops, build my walls and construct my tenements. From the dry land I steal winged and four-footed game, from the rivers I steal fish and turtles. There is nothing that I do not steal. For corn and grain, clay and wood, birds and beasts, fishes and turtles are all products of Nature. How can I claim them as mine?
